title: Can local areas do more to help people into work?
label: 18 November 2026 · Local employment support
summary: The committee examined plans to give local areas more responsibility for helping people find and keep work. The witnesses saw opportunities to connect employment support with health, skills and other local services, but warned that success would depend on adequate funding, local expertise, reliable data and clear responsibility when services fall short.

speakers.label: Chair
speakers.name: Debbie Abrahams
speakers.role: Chair of the Work and Pensions Committee

speakers.label: Professor Finn
speakers.name: Professor Dan Finn
speakers.role: Emeritus Professor of Social Inclusion, University of Portsmouth

glossary.definition: The government network of jobcentres that helps benefit claimants look for work and checks work-related requirements.
The transfer of decisions and responsibilities from central government to authorities covering particular areas.
Regional bodies, often led by mayors, that plan and manage services across several local council areas.
An employment-support programme delivered through local areas, particularly for people facing health-related barriers to work.
An employment-support programme for people who have been unemployed for a long time.
A review discussed throughout the hearing that proposed changes to support for young people entering work.
An organisation intended to help assess evidence about which approaches to local employment support work.

chapters.title: Why the system is centralised
chapters.takeaway: Jobcentres became closely tied to benefit claims, giving central government control but limiting how easily support fits with other local services.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Why is employment support so centrally run in the UK, and what does that mean in practice?

evidence.quote: The UK has a very centralised system for employment support. Could you explain how that has come about and what the pros and cons of it are?

turns.speaker: Professor Finn
turns.text: From the 1980s, governments increasingly directed jobcentres towards people claiming unemployment benefits and required those people to do more to look for work. As jobcentres took on more groups, including parents raising children alone and people on disability benefits, they became a service focused mainly on claimants rather than everyone looking for work.

evidence.quote: Over time, the Government basically harnessed and reformed the system to focus more on the claimant unemployed
people who are signing on and claiming benefits—the regular unemployed—should be required to do more things to look for work.

as the terms of reference of the jobcentre network have widened towards, first, lone parents, and then more recently, people on disability benefits, we have seen effectively a claimant employment service rather than a public employment service.

turns.speaker: Professor Finn
turns.text: That gives central government a way to try to reduce benefit spending and respond quickly to economic crises. But it also means Jobcentre Plus must keep checking that claimants meet work-related requirements, even as governments consider giving local areas more control.

evidence.quote: a service delivery mechanism that is primarily focused on getting the benefit bill down, as well as getting people into jobs
an instrument that is incredibly useful for central Government when they need to respond to crises and the arrival of economic shocks to the system.
I think that is one of the two tensions that are still there as we go into the next wave of localisation, which is the conditionality and sanctions regime.

turns.speaker: Dr Paxton
turns.text: The UK government is generally centralised, and the department that runs benefits also runs the jobcentre network. There's a difficult cycle: local areas may lack the staff and skills to take on support, but they often need responsibility in order to build those skills. Central and local government need to develop them together.

evidence.quote: the UK state in general is quite centralised
it is used to deliver the large network of jobcentres through the central Department

We say local areas do not have the capability and capacity to deliver that support, so we should not devolve it until they are ready to have it, but having some powers and responsibility is often important for building that capacity.
central Government working with subnational Government to develop capability and capacity.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Could national standards for good support still leave room for different local approaches?

evidence.quote: surely there needs to be an evidence-based approach that reflects those standards.

turns.speaker: Dr Paxton
turns.text: Yes. The question is how to set a minimum standard while letting areas connect employment help with services such as healthcare. Some areas, including Greater Manchester, have combined local programmes in different ways. We don't yet know the right balance between common standards and local flexibility.

evidence.quote: you can have those standards in place. There is then a balance with how you make sure that, combined with minimum standards of how you provide a service, you also give flexibility to get the benefits of that local approach and allow areas to set up a service in a way that does genuinely join up with other services locally, such as health services.
Greater Manchester, for example.
I do not think we yet know exactly what the right balance is there.

chapters.title: What moving decisions locally could change
chapters.takeaway: Other countries show that local control can make services easier to connect, but poorly designed funding can reward moving people off one benefit rather than into lasting work.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What could go wrong if local areas normally took the lead?

evidence.quote: What do you think are the risks associated with a devo-by-default design?

turns.speaker: Professor Finn
turns.text: Funding rules might reward an area for getting someone off one benefit, even if that person doesn't get a lasting job and moves onto another benefit paid for nationally. Finland found that this happened to some people during its experiments. Equally, a supportive programme still needs to be judged on whether it helps people into work.

evidence.quote: if you create the wrong kind of incentives for the local level, to get outcomes in a way that mean it is more important to get people off benefits rather than into a sustained job, those people can then pop up on other benefits.

One of the things that happened in Finland was that, as they experimented with devolving, they found that something like 10% of the people who were successfully taken off the caseload of municipalities ended up on other disability benefits that were funded by central Government.
On the ground, you might have very nice programmes that treat people very well, but do they get people into jobs?

turns.speaker: John Milne
turns.text: What can we learn from countries that have tried giving local areas more control?

evidence.quote: Looking at the international evidence for the relative success over decentralised versus centralised models, what can you tell us about that?

turns.speaker: Professor Finn
turns.text: Canada transferred programmes, staff and computer systems from a national employment service to provinces and local areas. Such changes can let local services work together better, but they take time and careful design. In particular, funding mustn't encourage authorities to turn people away from benefits instead of helping them into jobs.

evidence.quote: Canada, for instance, moved from a federal public employment service that covered the whole of the country to one that was devolved with staff transfers, IT transfers down to the level of provincial government and below provincial government to the local delivery units
these can improve things, but there are risks
place-based delivery systems that can join up services

Do you incentivise the local level to simply tell people to go away and not claim benefits because that keeps their bills down, keeps central Government’s bills down—those people pop up somewhere else—as opposed to the focus on getting people into employment?

turns.speaker: Professor Finn
turns.text: Canada also required provinces to assess their own programmes. Where provinces lacked the skills to do that, they worked with the national government at first. That helped them build the ability to judge results themselves in later agreements.

evidence.quote: they also devolved a requirement that people evaluated and assessed their own programmes and delivery.
other areas were required to develop joint evaluation frameworks with the centre in the initial periods and that built up the capacity of the local areas to deliver.
Then on the second iteration—these are usually three to five-year agreements—the areas were much better able to do these things themselves

turns.speaker: Dr Paxton
turns.text: Denmark offers another lesson: when local councils have clear responsibility for employment help, people know where to go. The UK's mix of locally run support and centrally run jobcentres could work, but it's less straightforward.

evidence.quote: In Denmark, where there is a high degree of devolution to municipalities in their wider employment support system, having that kind of single point of access is valuable for citizens to know where they can get support, and it is really clear who is responsible for the range of support.

we have some devolution to quite a high degree in employment support, perhaps for young people or disabled people, but then have jobcentres still running other parts of the employment system. It is not that that cannot work

turns.speaker: Dr Paxton
turns.text: Government plans also leave practical questions. It has said mayors should take responsibility for helping people who have been unemployed for a long time, while Restart is ending. Areas need to know what replaces it; gaps in support would hurt people who rely on it.

evidence.quote: We have the Restart scheme, which is coming to an end. “Rewiring the State” specifically said that employment support for the long-term unemployed would be devolved to mayors.
There is a history of gaps in employment support programmes, and that is bad for the people who rely on them to help get into work.

turns.speaker: Professor Finn
turns.text: We also need to watch what happens to the money. Scotland and Northern Ireland receive funding linked to the Restart budget without running a Restart programme. I can't tell from the available information where that money goes or whether outcomes differ. If budgets aren't set aside for a particular service, how do we make sure people still receive it?

evidence.quote: At the moment, there is a Barnett consequential for Scotland and Northern Ireland with the Restart budget, but there is no Restart programme in either country
you just cannot find out where the money has gone, because it is not ringfenced; it just dissipates into the system.
Well, exactly, and that might be a good question to ask Ministers, because I do not know.
The dilemma is then how do you steer to make sure that people are getting the services you want them to get?

chapters.title: People, money and responsibility
chapters.takeaway: Local authorities will need skilled staff, usable information and stable funding, while national government must decide how much freedom and financial risk to give them.

turns.speaker: Liz Twist
turns.text: Can strategic authorities take on employment support while also gaining responsibilities for things such as transport and housing?

evidence.quote: At the same time as the strategic authorities are taking on responsibility for employment support, they are also getting new devolved functions from transport through to housing.

turns.speaker: Dr Paxton
turns.text: It'll vary by area. The next transfer of responsibilities may happen faster than the gradual changes in places already doing this work. Authorities particularly need people who can design support around local needs, use data to test whether it works, and buy services from outside organisations on sensible terms.

evidence.quote: It will vary substantially.
The next stage would see a much faster roll-out of the capability needed to deliver these employment support programmes.
Our research found three particular capability gaps
One is policy design capability.
A second gap is around analytical capability.
The third area where we think capability needs to be strong is the commercial capability to go out and procure services

turns.speaker: Professor Finn
turns.text: Local authorities already buy and manage many services, so we shouldn't overlook their expertise. But the transition will be uneven. The department that runs jobcentres should share what it has learned, and local leaders must build their own teams quickly.

evidence.quote: DWP has good commercial expertise that it has developed over many years. How do you share that?
We should not underestimate the amount of acumen that exists at local and strategic authority levels. The authorities buy lots of services already
there is a transitional phase that we will have to go through, where it will be very uneven.
it is the responsibility of both centre and the strategic authorities themselves to build up that acumen.

turns.speaker: Professor Finn
turns.text: Local teams also need access to information showing where help is needed and whether it works. Sharing that information between organisations remains a real problem.

evidence.quote: The local level has to have a line of sight of a lot of this information to be able to track where it needs to target services and then evaluate and assess the impact of the services it is delivering
data sharing is a real bugbear in the system.

turns.speaker: Dr Paxton
turns.text: One option is to lend experienced national staff to local authorities for a period. But people who have run national contracts won't necessarily have all the answers for local delivery; local areas have expertise of their own.

evidence.quote: the potential use of secondments from central Government into strategic and local authorities to help support.
we should not always assume that people who have worked in central Government have all the answers. A lot of expertise already exists at local and strategic authority level.

turns.speaker: Liz Twist
turns.text: Local government budgets are already under pressure. Will the money transferred with these new responsibilities be enough?

evidence.quote: local government budgets, which are already under massive pressure. What do you think are the resource implications for local government as it takes on responsibility for employment support? Will any additional funding that is provided be enough to match those demands?

turns.speaker: Professor Finn
turns.text: There's a choice between reserving money for a particular national programme and giving local areas freedom to spend it differently. Some countries let local authorities keep savings if they help people into work faster, but make them cover extra benefit costs if they overspend. That can encourage action, yet Finland shows it can also leave authorities paying charges instead of providing services.

evidence.quote: Do you try to ringfence the money? In which case, are you then just simply making the local level a deliverer of national programmes
If you manage to get people in work more quickly, you keep the additional resource that is in that block grant
if you overspend, you have to make up the difference from your own resources.
some local authorities are finding that they have these fines, effectively, and that means they cannot provide services because they are paying these fines.

turns.speaker: Dr Paxton
turns.text: Another risk is promising people a very specific level of support without paying for it. Authorities may then concentrate on meeting the promise rather than doing what most improves people's chances. Minimum standards can matter, but they must fit with the funding and the results government wants.

evidence.quote: A second risk is around piling on legal entitlements or guarantees in a system without providing the funding for it.
There is a role sometimes for minimum standards and making sure that people are delivering a certain standard of support and ensuring access to it.

if you make those guarantees on minimum standards too specific and onerous without providing the funding, you skew service provision towards just meeting standards rather than actually delivering better outcomes

chapters.title: Making local services work together
chapters.takeaway: Support may work better when employment, health and skills services cooperate around people's needs, but local relationships and clear responsibilities matter as much as organisational plans.

turns.speaker: Andrew Pakes
turns.text: If this involves more than passing powers from one level of government to another, what do we gain by involving more organisations?

evidence.quote: we are not just talking about devolution as going from one tier of government to another but opening up to a much wider set of stakeholders being involved. Do you have any reflections on the benefits and shortcomings of doing this.

turns.speaker: Dr Paxton
turns.text: Someone may be out of work for several connected reasons, including health, housing, skills or poverty. Local services should respond to the person rather than treat finding a job as a separate problem. That takes people in different organisations working together, funding they can use flexibly, and enough stability to build those relationships.

evidence.quote: they might be around skills, health, housing and poverty or other experiences that they have had.
We should try to design services that work around individuals and their multiple needs.
it so often depends on individuals who know each other and work together
Having that local flexibility and long-term funding is important

turns.speaker: Professor Finn
turns.text: That cooperation still needs organisations clearly responsible for making it happen, usually the employment service and local government. In Manchester, local teams identified poor dental health as a barrier to work and arranged help involving university dental trainees. I don't know what happened to that particular service later, but it shows what local organisations can spot together.

evidence.quote: you need a couple of key agencies that have core responsibility for steering the system. In most of the countries that I have looked at, effectively the public employment service is one of those key agencies. The municipal level, local authority government is the other kind of agency.
oral health was a massive barrier for people getting back into work
They organised a service with the university dental technicians and trainees, and started to provide a service. Unfortunately, it is really hard to find out what happened to that service afterwards

turns.speaker: Andrew Pakes
turns.text: Where do employers fit into a locally run system?

evidence.quote: Can you both say a bit more about what role there is for employers in this new world led by strategic authorities?

turns.speaker: Dr Paxton
turns.text: A strategic authority may be large enough to work with major regional employers while local councils also work with smaller businesses. A clearer local employment service could give employers a better place to find recruits than today's patchwork of programmes. But basic standards for helping employees with ill health should probably be national, because big employers operate across area boundaries.

evidence.quote: operating at a scale that allows them to engage with big employers in their region
Convening large businesses as well as small businesses working with local authorities
Those standards should probably be national wherever possible, because a lot of these larger employers are working across strategic authority boundaries.
The current patchwork of various different programmes, and jobcentres not necessarily being places that employers feel they want to go to fill vacancies, is a problem at the moment

turns.speaker: Professor Finn
turns.text: Employers also need practical help filling jobs. If several small providers all approach the same businesses, that can put employers off. A coordinated service could find vacancies, arrange short training for people who have been on benefits, and respond to local employers' needs.

evidence.quote: New supermarkets open in an area, so how do we train up a whole bunch of people that might have been on benefits for a long time? We can do two, four, six-week training courses to get people prepared.
If you have lots of small organisations on different contracts competing for the jobs that are out there, it can be off-putting to employers
They are key skill people who go out and find vacancies for the people that need placements.

turns.speaker: Andrew Pakes
turns.text: But how local is local? Could creating a regional organisation draw money and decisions away from councils and neighbourhood services?

evidence.quote: How local is local? My worry is that you set up a strategic bureaucracy to deliver this, which takes money directly away.
How do you think the division between that devolution at a strategic level to local authorities should work

turns.speaker: Dr Paxton
turns.text: An area can agree shared priorities while delivering help much closer to people, sometimes through trusted neighbourhood centres. We'll need to learn from Connect to Work how different arrangements between strategic authorities and councils have actually worked.

evidence.quote: Hopefully through the Connect to Work programme evaluation, we will get more of a sense of how that has and has not worked in different areas
having a shared vision for what your local system would look like within a wider strategic area but then giving flexibility locally.
employment support is being delivered not at a local authority level but at a much more neighbourhood level.
using trusted community centres and trusted individuals within that area.

turns.speaker: Professor Finn
turns.text: We shouldn't assume every regional authority can easily bring its councils together. Some areas have longstanding political cooperation; others have rivalries. And organisations are being reorganised while their staff are expected to improve services, which makes the change harder.

evidence.quote: the amount of institutional churn that is taking place throughout a lot of the structures on which these expectations are being built
There is a whole bunch of people out there who are not sure which job they will have in six months’ time
the most progress has been made where there are mainly urban areas, political consensus and a long experience of authorities working together.
areas that may not be used to working together, or where there is interlocal rivalries and competition between each other.

turns.speaker: Andrew Pakes
turns.text: What about people with specialised needs who form a small group in any one area? Might national support still be better for them?

evidence.quote: Do you have any thoughts on keeping national provision where there are very specific needs that may be very specialised, or where there may be economies of scale by having a national programme?

turns.speaker: Dr Paxton
turns.text: It depends on the group. A strategic authority covers more people than a single council and could probably organise most specialist services, but I wouldn't rule out exceptions. We need to consider each kind of support on its own merits.

evidence.quote: the level at which that provision is best done will vary depending on the size of the group.

it probably must be more of a case-by-case approach for different groups, but I think in general strategic authorities are probably at the level at which you could organise most specialist services for most groups.
there will be lots of specific examples of groups that will not be served by that model

turns.speaker: Professor Finn
turns.text: Devolution doesn't stop national government stepping in if a group is poorly served, or funding a specialist programme itself. Evaluation should reveal who isn't getting effective help and why.

evidence.quote: when you devolve, you do not forgo the right for the centre to intervene if you are delivering for particular kinds of groups.
Why did it not work for them? What has the level of service been directed towards them? Does it need to be more specialised and so on?
central Government retains the right to intervene directly or to have a separate programme.

chapters.title: How to tell if support works
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses wanted public results, accounts from people using services and quicker evaluation—not just counts of how many people entered a programme.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: As more areas design their own support, how should we judge whether it's successful?

evidence.quote: What are your group of success metrics at a national level and what metrics could be used at a local level?

turns.speaker: Professor Finn
turns.text: Look at both results and people's experience: did they get a job, keep it and earn more, and what help did they actually receive? Restart surveys participants, but those findings aren't public. We also lack similarly systematic public information about people's experiences in jobcentres.

evidence.quote: I think it must be a combination of outcomes and experience.
in the Restart programme, there are participant surveys going on there of people’s experiences.
in the Restart thing, they are not public.
We do not have insight into the experience of the people using jobcentres in that systematic way.
employment, sustained employment, earnings gains

turns.speaker: Professor Finn
turns.text: We need information quickly enough to fix problems during a programme, not only a study years later. And local jobcentre results should be public so people can compare areas that face similar conditions. Taking money away from a struggling area may make it less able to improve.

evidence.quote: What we need now is whether it is working, or why it is not working and how we can we fix it.
local jobcentre performance is publicly available
You are not comparing rural and urban but urban and urban
if you have a poorly performing area and you take money away from it, it is hardly likely to be able to improve performance.

turns.speaker: Dr Paxton
turns.text: Areas should be able to try a different approach if they explain why it might work locally and test the results. If things go badly wrong, national government must still be able to work with an area or step in. Local committees also need information and resources to question their leaders.

evidence.quote: it is reasonable for areas to say, “We are going to take a slightly different approach to what the best evidence shows us so far”. It is very important that there is a good justification for that
strong evaluation to make sure that people are monitoring how outcomes are going
for central Government to step in or at least work alongside areas to try to turn outcomes around.
local scrutiny committees are part of a really strong local accountability system. They will need data, and resources to scrutinise that data and hold their area to account

turns.speaker: Neil Duncan-Jordan
turns.text: Can other countries show us how to measure real results rather than just the number of people going through a service?

evidence.quote: Are there lessons that the UK could learn from other countries about how we measure the outcomes of success, rather than the inputs that you mentioned earlier, to ensure proper accountability and delivery?

turns.speaker: Professor Finn
turns.text: In the United States, earnings records help show not just who starts work but how their pay changes afterwards. Linking tax and benefit information here could improve comparisons between programmes. But records alone miss people who don't claim benefits; surveys can help show what happens to them.

evidence.quote: it enables you to capture not just the people who are getting jobs, but what the earnings gain is over a period
The integration of tax and benefit records, for example, is a classic one.
there is a whole population out there who do not claim benefits who are economically inactive
The best way is surveys.

turns.speaker: Professor Finn
turns.text: Some local claims about successful programmes rely heavily on what providers report, without enough independent checking. A What Works Centre could help, but its guidance needs to arrive while areas can still use it.

evidence.quote: We are relying a lot on what providers are saying. There is no audit test or trail in it, but the results look great. That is not evaluation
hopefully the What Works Centre can do it.
My message is that the What Works Centre needs to produce stuff that is real time.

turns.speaker: Dr Paxton
turns.text: There's another limit to the evidence: past health-related programmes often tested support among a small group who chose to join. Their results may not tell us what will happen if local areas reach many more people, including those less willing to engage. Local delivery might help, but we don't know; it needs testing.

evidence.quote: employment support programmes today have only engaged a very small minority of the total group of people who are out of work due to ill health.
our evidence base does not necessarily carry across to a programme that is trying to engage a much broader swathe of people
it is possible, if the system is delivered at a more local level, that people might be more willing to engage. We do not know that, but that should be a focus of evaluation.

chapters.title: The promise and the pressure
chapters.takeaway: Both witnesses saw promise in local support, but warned against expecting reorganising authorities to produce fast results without the capacity to deliver.

turns.speaker: Steve Darling
turns.text: Looking ahead, what gives you hope about this change, and what worries you?

evidence.quote: What are your hopes and fears over the next few years around how central Government could or should approach this way forward?

turns.speaker: Professor Finn
turns.text: I think the direction is right. I've seen employment advisers working more closely with health services, including talking-therapy services and GPs, in ways I hadn't seen before. My fear is that the ambitions exceed what these organisations can deliver soon. If expectations are too high, people may call the change a failure after only a couple of years.

evidence.quote: Personally I think it is moving in the right direction in general.
everything from putting employment advisers into health settings, talking therapies through to GPs. This is new.

the ambition far outstrips the capacity of these structures to deliver. If you create false expectations, it will be very easy in two years’ time for people to turn around and say, “This has not worked”.

turns.speaker: Dr Paxton
turns.text: My hope is a less confusing system that connects employment, health and other local help. My fear is that areas try different ideas but nobody properly tests which ones work. Evaluation needs to be planned from the start, with useful lessons shared between areas.

evidence.quote: My biggest hope is that it brings some coherence to a system that, at the moment, is just very messy and a complete patchwork.
A particular hope I have around the collaboration between health and employment and other services
One of my fears is that areas take lots of different approaches, but we do not set up the evaluation architecture to understand what works.

ensuring that evaluation is built into the start as new programmes are set up locally; in co-ordinating evaluation across different areas; and, really importantly for helping ensure minimum standards without having minimum standards, in sharing best practice across areas.
